text:
**The Surveyor**

The road had been closed since the spring washout, which was why Arthur Lind was walking on it. He was sixty-three and had spent thirty-one years measuring land for people who wanted to know where it ended. Now he liked to walk where no one could ask him anything. The county had put up a sawhorse and a sign at the lower gate, and he had stepped around both with the small, private satisfaction of a man breaking a rule no one would ever enforce.

It was late September, the hour when the light turns the color of weak tea. The aspens along the switchbacks had begun to go yellow from the top down, as if something were slowly being poured into them. He had been climbing for three hours. His knees had opinions about it. He was thinking about nothing in particular, a sandwich, the word "escarpment," whether he had left the stove on, when he noticed that the guardrail at the fourth bend was gone.

Not gone, exactly. Folded. A length of it lay peeled back like the lid of a sardine tin, and beyond it the slope fell away through broken fir saplings to a shelf of rock sixty feet down. On the shelf was a small blue car, on its side, one rear wheel still turning.

He stood without moving. This was not indecision. It was the instinct of a man who had learned that the first thing to do on uncertain ground was to look at it carefully. Then he took off his pack and went down.

It was not a graceful descent. He went on his heels and the heels of his hands, and twice he sat down hard and slid. The smell reached him first: coolant, hot metal, the green, bruised smell of crushed pine. The wheel had stopped by the time he got there.

She was still belted into the driver's seat, which was now more of a wall. A woman, maybe forty, maybe younger, in a gray fleece zipped to her chin, dark hair fallen across her face. The windshield was gone. He did not need to reach through it to know, but he did anyway, two fingers against her neck, cool and not yet cold. He held them there long enough to be fair about it.

"I'm sorry," he said. His voice sounded too small in the open air, like something dropped into a well.

He climbed back up for the device his daughter had given him two Christmases ago, a yellow thing the size of a deck of cards that talked to satellites. He had never used it. It had a cover over the red button, like in films about missiles. He pressed it, and a message came back after a minute: *SOS received. Responders notified.* A second asked whether he was safe. He typed slowly with his thumb, *one deceased, no others visible, I will wait,* and then *Upper Fork road, mile 9.* The reply said help was on the way, two to four hours.

He went back down and sat on a flat rock a little way from the car, upwind. He considered leaving her. There was nothing to be done, and the cold would come up out of the valley soon. But standing on the road like a man waiting for a bus seemed a kind of lie about what had happened. Someone should be with her. It was not a belief he could have defended, and he would have been embarrassed to say it to anyone who could answer.

So he said it to her.

"I'm going to stay," he said. "They said a few hours. I hope that's all right."

The mountain seemed to take this in. Above the shelf the fir forest stood close and dark. A raven went over, said one thing, and thought better of it. Somewhere below, a creek was working at its slow business of removing the mountain a grain at a time.

"I'm a surveyor," he said after a while. "Was. I'm retired now, which my ex-wife says is just surveying with no one paying you."

He almost stopped. But the quiet asked to be filled, and he had never been able to stand a silence he was responsible for.

He told her about his first job, in Wyoming, at twenty-two, holding the rod for a man named Delbert Voss, who chewed toothpicks to pulp and could not abide a crooked line. Voss used to say the land didn't know it was owned. "Fences are just things we say to each other," Voss said, and Arthur had thought it the wisest sentence he'd ever heard, and had spent thirty years finding out it was merely true.

The shadow of the ridge crossed the car and the rock and his boots. He zipped his jacket. Then he climbed to the car again and reached through the empty frame of the windshield to push the hair gently back from her face. She had a small scar through her left eyebrow. He did not know why this was a relief. He supposed it was that she had been someone with a history, a bicycle or a staircase or a brother with a stick, and not just a thing that had happened on a Tuesday.

On the dash, a pair of sunglasses sat where they had always been. That was the odd thing, how much had stayed. The crash had been selective, as weather is, taking the guardrail and the windshield and leaving the sunglasses.

"My father had a hardware store," he told her, sitting again. "In Ohio. He sold nails by the pound out of wooden bins, and he'd always add two or three after the scale balanced. I asked him why. He said, 'So they leave thinking they got a deal.' The store's a vape shop now. I stood in the doorway like a ghost who's been given the wrong address."

He laughed a little, and the laugh frightened a pair of jays out of the fir.

"I don't mean to be morbid," he said. "It's only that I've been thinking how much of what I thought was solid was just slow. The store was slow. My marriage took twenty-six years to end. Mountains are slow. That one"—he nodded across the valley at the long gray ridge, going violet—"has been coming down since before anything we'd call a person. It's the same as the car. It's just that the car was fast."

The cold came up, as he had known it would. He put on his hat and, after a while, his gloves.

"What I'm trying to say," he said, and stopped. He had wanted to say something useful to her, some comfort that was not a lie, and had found that the only true comfort he had was that nothing stays where it is put. The hour, the wreck, the long afternoon in which he sat telling a stranger about nails was already becoming the past, and the past, whatever else you could say against it, was safe. It could not be hurt anymore.

That did not sound like comfort when he put it that way. He said, instead, "I'm glad it was a nice day."

It had been. He told her so. The sky over the shelf had gone clear and enormous, and the first star was out above the ridge, one he could never remember the name of. The aspens higher up were still lit, a last band of gold against the fir. If one had to be anywhere, he said, this was not the worst place.

He sat on, and the dark settled in the way water fills a footprint.

At some point he realized he was listening for it, and had been for a while: a flat, far-off chop in the air, so faint he took it for his own pulse. It grew. A light swung across the far slope, searching, and then found the road and the bent rail and held there, white and impersonal and kind.

He stood. His knees objected. He looked at the shape of her behind the glass that was no longer there, and felt, absurdly, that he ought to introduce himself properly, as he would have at a door.

"Arthur," he said. "Arthur Lind."

The helicopter was over the ridge now, and the aspens began to shake in the downdraft, all their small coins of leaves turning at once. Some drifted down over the shelf and settled on the roof of the car, and on the rock, and on his shoulders. He did not brush them off. He lifted one arm and waved, so they would know where he was, and stood waiting in the loud light, with the whole dark mountain behind him, and the creek going on below, taking its time.
